documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Work Part A first.  You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B.  You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work.  Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper.  Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem.  For example,

  Doe, Jamie

  A1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used.  Its memory must be cleared of data and programs.  You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator.  Calculators may not be shared.  Cell phones, PDA’s, or cameras may not be used during the exam or while the exam papers are present. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Do not discuss the contents of this exam with anyone until after the submission deadline.
- Good luck!

problems.title: A1
problems.statement: The capacitors in the circuit diagrammed to the right are initially uncharged.

figures.alt: Circuit: a 6.00V battery with switch S and a 10.0 Ω resistor in the left branch; a 20.0 Ω resistor in the middle branch; in the right branch a 4.00 μF capacitor, a 30.0 Ω resistor and a 2.00 μF capacitor in series.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the current in each resistor immediately after the switch labeled S is closed?
parts.statementAfter: After a very long time, the capacitors are fully charged.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the current in each resistor at this time?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: What is the charge on each capacitor?

answer.note: Both capacitors carry the same charge, Q₂ = Q₄ = 5.33 μC.

solution.statement:
a. At the instant the switch is closed, there is no charge on the capacitor and no voltage across it. Applying Kirchhoff’s junction rule $I_{10} = I_{20} + I_{30}$.

Applying Kirchhoff’s loop rule to the right loop $0 = (20.0\ \Omega)I_{20} - (30.0\ \Omega)I_{30}$.

Solving for $I_{20}$ and then $I_{10}$, $I_{20} = 1.5I_{30}$ $\quad I_{10} = 1.5I_{30} + I_{30} = 2.5I_{30}$

Applying Kirchhoff’s loop rule to the left loop

$$0 = 6.00\ \mathrm{V} - (20.0\ \Omega)I_{20} - (10.0\ \Omega)I_{10} = 6.00\ \mathrm{V} - (20.0\ \Omega)(1.5I_{30}) - (10.0\ \Omega)(2.5I_{30})$$

$$0 = 6.00\ \mathrm{V} - (30.0\ \Omega)I_{30} - (25.0\ \Omega)I_{30} = 6.00\ \mathrm{V} - (55.0\ \Omega)I_{30}$$

Solving for the currents $I_{30} = \dfrac{6.00\ \mathrm{V}}{55.0\ \Omega} = 0.109\ \mathrm{A}$. $\quad I_{20} = 1.5(0.109\ \mathrm{A}) = 0.164\ \mathrm{A}$

and $I_{10} = 2.5(0.109\ \mathrm{A}) = 0.273\ \mathrm{A}$

*$\{$A solution using parallel and series resistor combinations is equally valid.$\}$*

b. When the switch has been closed for a very long time, the capacitors are fully charged. Current no longer flows in the capacitor branch and $I_{30} = 0$

Applying Kirchhoff’s loop rule to the left loop

$$0 = 6.00\ \mathrm{V} - (20.0\ \Omega)I_{10} - (10.0\ \Omega)I_{10} = 6.00\ \mathrm{V} - (30.0\ \Omega)I_{10}$$

$$I_{20} = I_{10} = \frac{6.00\ \mathrm{V}}{30.0\ \Omega} = 0.200\ \mathrm{A}$$

c. The two capacitors are in series. Both have the same charge. The equivalent capacitance is

$$\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_4} = \frac{1}{2.00\ \mu\mathrm{F}} + \frac{1}{4.00\ \mu\mathrm{F}} = \frac{3}{4.00\ \mu\mathrm{F}}$$

or $$C_{eq} = 1.33\ \mu\mathrm{F}.$$

The voltage across the equivalent capacitance is the same as that across the 20.0 Ω resistor.

$$V_c = V_{20} = (20.0\ \Omega)I_{20} = (20.0\ \Omega)(0.200\ \mathrm{A}) = 4.00\ \mathrm{V}.$$

So the charge $$Q_2 = Q_4 = Q_{eq} = C_{eq}V_c = (1.33\ \mu\mathrm{F})(4.00\ \mathrm{V}) = 5.33\ \mu\mathrm{C}$$

problems.title: A2
problems.statement: A hot air balloon with average density 1.20 kg/m$^3$ is in equilibrium at a height of 1.00 km above sea level.  A gust of wind pushes the balloon to a height of 1.10 km above sea level and releases it at rest.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: How long does it take for the balloon to return to its equilibrium position?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: How fast is it going when it passes through equilibrium?

problems.statementAfterParts:
Assume that:  The atmospheric density is a linear function of height.

The balloon volume and average density are constant.

Variations in the gravitational field with height are negligible.

The density of air at sea level is 1.29 kg/m$^3$.

Drag is negligible.

solution.statement:
A2. First find the forces on the balloon. The weight force is

$$W = mg = \rho_b Vg$$

where $\rho_b = 1.20\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is the density of the balloon, $V$ is its volume, and $g$ is the gravitational field strength. The buoyant force is

$$B = \rho_a Vg$$

where $\rho_a$ is the density of air. Since it is assumed to be a linear function of height, $\rho_a = \rho_0 - \alpha h$ where $\rho_0 = 1.29\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is the density of air at sea level and $h$ is the height above sea level. The forces are in equilibrium at $h_0 = 1.00\ \mathrm{km} = 1.00 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{m}$.

$$\rho_b Vg = \rho_a Vg = (\rho_0 - \alpha h_0)Vg. \qquad (\mathrm{A2-1})$$

Solving this for $\alpha$, $$\alpha = \frac{\rho_0 - \rho_b}{h_0} = \frac{1.29\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} - 1.20\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}}{1000\ \mathrm{m}} = 9 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kg/m^4}$$

a. After being blown to a height of $h = 1.10$ km, the forces are no longer balanced.

$$ma = B - W$$

$$\rho_b Va = (\rho_0 - \alpha h)Vg - \rho_b Vg.$$

Substituting (A2 – 1) into the above equation

$$\rho_b Va = (\rho_0 - \alpha h)Vg - (\rho_0 - \alpha h_0)Vg = -\alpha(h - h_0)Vg = -\alpha\Delta h Vg.$$

Solving for the acceleration $a$ $$a = -\left(\frac{\alpha g}{\rho_b}\right)\Delta h.$$

The acceleration is proportional to the displacement. The motion is simple harmonic motion with

$$\omega = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\alpha g}{\rho_b}\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{(9 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kg/m^4})(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2})}{1.20\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}}} = 0.0271\ \mathrm{rad/s}.$$

The balloon is released at rest at amplitude $A = h - h_0 = 100$ m and first passes through its equilibrium position at a time equal to one fourth its period.

$$t = \frac{T}{4} = \frac{2\pi}{4\omega} = \frac{\pi}{2(0.0271\ \mathrm{rad/s})} = 57.9\ \mathrm{s}.$$

b. The balloon passes through its equilibrium position with maximum velocity

$$v = \omega A = (0.0271\ \mathrm{rad/s})(100\ \mathrm{m}) = 2.71\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

figures.alt: Free-body diagram of the balloon: a circle with an upward arrow labelled B and a downward arrow labelled W.

problems.title: A3
problems.statement: Sound sources S$_1$ and S$_2$ are located at $+x_0$ and $–x_0$, respectively.  The sources produce tones with the same phase and amplitude.  The frequency can be varied from 175 Hz to 625 Hz, but both speakers have the same frequency.  Use 340 m/s for the velocity of sound in air and $x_0 = 0.850$ m.

figures.alt: An x-axis with a y-axis arrow at the origin; source S2 marked by a dot at –x0 and source S1 at +x0.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: For which frequency or frequencies in the above range is minimum sound intensity heard at all points along the $x$-axis with $x > x_0$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Next consider the region on the $x$-axis between the two sound sources S$_1$ and S$_2$.  Assuming that the amplitude $A$ does not decrease with distance from the source, write an equation that gives the resultant sound wavefunction in the form $\Psi(x,t) = 2A\psi(x)\phi(t)$, where $\psi$ and $\phi$ are functions of $x$ and $t$, respectively.  The equation may also depend on the wavelength $\lambda$ and frequency $f$ of the sound waves and should be valid for all points on the $x$-axis with $-x_0 < x < +x_0$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: For the frequency or frequencies found in Part (a), at which points between $x = –\ 0.85$ m and $x = +0.85$ m does minimum sound intensity occur?

solution.statement:
A3. a. In order for minimum sound intensity to be heard in the region along the $x$-axis with $x > x_0$, the distance between sources must be an odd half-integer multiple of the wavelength $\lambda$.

$$2x_0 = (2n - 1)\frac{\lambda}{2} = (2n - 1)\frac{v}{2f} \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$

where $v = 340\ \mathrm{m/s}$, the velocity of sound in air, and $175\ \mathrm{Hz} \le f \le 625\ \mathrm{Hz}$, the frequency of the sound that produces minimum intensity. Solving for the frequency

$$f_n = (2n - 1)\frac{v}{4x_0} = (2n - 1)\frac{(340\ \mathrm{m/s})}{4(0.85\ \mathrm{m})} = (2n - 1)(100\ \mathrm{Hz}).$$

The frequencies in the possible range are

$f_2 = 300\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_3 = 500\ \mathrm{Hz}$

b. In the region between the sources, source S$_1$ emits a wave $\Psi_1$ that travels to the left and source S$_2$ emits a wave $\Psi_2$ that travels to the right.

$$\Psi_1 = A\sin(\omega t + k(x - x_0)) \qquad \Psi_2 = A\sin(\omega t - k(x + x_0))$$

where $k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$ and $\omega = 2\pi f$.

Adding the waves to determine the resultant wave

$$\Psi = \Psi_1 + \Psi_2 = A\sin(\omega t + k(x - x_0)) + A\sin(\omega t - k(x + x_0))$$

$$\Psi = A\sin(\omega t - kx_0)\cos(kx) + A\cos(\omega t - kx_0)\sin(kx)$$

$$+ A\sin(\omega t - kx_0)\cos(kx) - A\cos(\omega t - kx_0)\sin(kx)$$

$$\Psi = 2A\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t - kx_0)$$

Note: This equation has the correct $x$-dependence. The waves travel the same distance to reach $x = 0$. This point is an interference maximum. Any expression with

$$\Psi = 2A\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t - kx_0 + \delta)$$

where $\delta$ is a phase constant is valid.

c. Minimum sound intensity occurs when $\cos(kx) = 0$, i.e., $kx = \pm(2n + 1)\pi/2$. Solving for $x$,

$$x = \pm\frac{(2n + 1)\pi}{2k} = \pm\frac{(2n + 1)\pi}{2(2\pi/\lambda)} = \pm\frac{(2n + 1)\lambda}{4} = \pm\frac{(2n + 1)v}{4f}$$

For $f = 300$ Hz: $$x = \pm\frac{(2n + 1)(340\ \mathrm{m/s})}{4(300\ \mathrm{Hz})} = \pm(2n + 1)(0.283\ \mathrm{m}) = \pm 0.283\ \mathrm{m} \qquad \text{with } n = 0.$$

For $f = 500$ Hz: $$x = \pm\frac{(2n + 1)(340\ \mathrm{m/s})}{4(500\ \mathrm{Hz})} = \pm(2n + 1)(0.170\ \mathrm{m}) = \pm 0.170\ \mathrm{m},\ \pm 0.510\ \mathrm{m}$$

with $n = 0, 1$.

problems.title: A4
problems.statement: A ball is thrown so that it hits a stationary ramp and then bounces up the ramp.  Immediately before the first collision between the ball and the ramp, the ball has a velocity $v_\mathrm{o}$ that is horizontal as shown in the accompanying diagram.  Assume that all collisions are perfectly elastic, that there is no friction between the ramp and the ball, and that air resistance is negligible.  At the instant that the ball makes its $N$+1$^{\mathrm{st}}$ collision with the ramp, the ball is moving perpendicular to the ramp.  Express your answers in terms of $N$, $v_\mathrm{o}$, and $g$.

figures.alt: A right-triangle ramp rising to the right; a horizontal arrow labelled vo points at the lower part of the incline.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the angle that the ramp makes with the horizontal.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the distance, measured along the ramp, between the point at which the first collision occurs and the point at which the $N$+1$^{\mathrm{st}}$ collision occurs?

solution.statement:
A4. Selecting the $y$-axis perpendicular to the ramp and the $x$-axis parallel to the ramp in the upward direction, the components of the gravitational acceleration are

$a_x = -g\sin\theta$ and $a_y = -g\cos\theta$,

where $\theta$ is the angle the ramp makes with the horizontal. The components of the initial velocity are $v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$ and $v_{0y} = -v_0\sin\theta$.

a. At each collision with the plane, the $x$-component of velocity does not change while the $y$-component reverses sign. At the start of the first bounce $v_{0y} = +v_0\sin\theta$.

The $y$-displacement is given by $$y = y_0 + v_{0y}t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_y t^2 \qquad (\mathrm{A4-1})$$

Let $y_0 = 0$ at $t = 0$, the start of the first bounce. Let $t = t_1$, the time when the ball returns to the ramp $y = 0$, at the end of the first bounce. Substituting these values into (A4 – 1)

$$0 = v_0\sin\theta t_1 - \tfrac{1}{2}g\cos\theta t_1^2.$$

Solving for $t_1$ and eliminating the initial time $t_1 = 0$, $$t_1 = \frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g\cos\theta} = \frac{2v_0}{g}\tan\theta.$$

The velocity at the end of the first bounce, as the ball is about to impact the ramp again, is

$$v_y = v_{0y} + a_y t = v_0\sin\theta - g\cos\theta t = v_0\sin\theta - g\cos\theta\frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g\cos\theta} = -v_0\sin\theta.$$

Upon hitting the ramp the velocity reverses to become $v_{0y} = +v_0\sin\theta$.

Each bounce has the same $v_{0y}$ and $a_y$, so each bounce takes the same amount of time $t_1$.

Therefore the time for $N$ bounces is $$t_N = Nt = N\frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g\cos\theta} = \frac{2Nv_0}{g}\tan\theta. \qquad (\mathrm{A4-2})$$

There is no impulse in the $x$-direction, so the $x$-equations hold continuously. At the end of the Nth bounce, the ball’s velocity is perpendicular to the ramp, $v_x = 0$. Substituting this into the equation for the $x$-component of velocity,

$$v_x = v_{0x} + a_x t$$

$$0 = v_0\cos\theta - g\sin\theta t_N = v_0\cos\theta - g\sin\theta\left(N\frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g\cos\theta}\right).$$

Dividing by $v_0\cos\theta$, $$0 = 1 - \frac{2N\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} = 1 - 2N\tan^2\theta.$$

Solving for $\tan\theta$ $$\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2N}} \qquad (\mathrm{A4-3})$$

b. The x-displacement is given by $x = v_{0x}t + \frac{1}{2}a_x t^2$.

The maximum displacement occurs at the end of the Nth bounce, time $t_N$. Combining (A4 – 2) and (A4 – 3) $$t_N = \frac{2Nv_0}{g}\tan\theta = \frac{2Nv_0}{g}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2N}} = \frac{v_0}{g}\sqrt{2N}.$$

Substituting this into the x-equation,

$$x = (v_0\cos\theta)\left(\frac{v_0}{g}\sqrt{2N}\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}(-g\sin\theta)\left(\frac{v_0}{g}\sqrt{2N}\right)^2 = \frac{v_0^2}{g}\cos\theta\sqrt{2N} - \frac{v_0^2}{2g}2N\sin\theta$$

Using the triangle to the right to determine $\cos\theta$ and $\sin\theta$

$$\cos\theta = \sqrt{\frac{2N}{2n + 1}} \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2N - 1}}$$

$$x = \frac{v_0^2}{g}\sqrt{\frac{2N}{2N + 1}}\sqrt{2N} - \frac{v_0^2}{2g}2N\frac{1}{\sqrt{2N + 1}} = \frac{v_0^2}{g}\frac{N}{\sqrt{2N + 1}}$$

figures.alt: Right triangle with angle θ at the left vertex: hypotenuse labelled √(2N+1), horizontal leg labelled √(2N), vertical leg labelled 1.

figures.caption: Figure 1-1
figures.alt: Figure 1-1: an electron gun with accelerating potential V sends electrons e- into a grey cloud H of hydrogen; scattered electrons pass through a series of parallel plates with aligned holes and curve in a magnetic field B (pointing out of the page) onto the final plate.

figures.caption: Figure 1-2
figures.alt: Figure 1-2: the developed film showing the entrance hole (open circle, labelled “hole through which electrons entered”) and a row of spots; the distances from the hole to the two most distant spots are marked 3.980 cm and 9.491 cm.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement:
In 1913, Niels Bohr first derived a formula for the energy levels of the hydrogen atom.  He postulated that the single electron orbited a very massive proton under the influence of the electrostatic force and that the circular electron orbits had quantized angular momentum

$$L = n\hbar = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$$

where $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ and $h$ is Planck’s constant.  These postulates gave rise to discrete values of the electron’s total energy $E_n$.  Derive these Bohr Model energy levels. Express your answer in terms of Coulomb’s constant $k$, the electron mass $m$, the electron charge $e$, $\hbar$, and $n$.  If done correctly, your answer should evaluate to

$$E_n = -\frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}}{n^2} = -\frac{13.6\ \mathrm{eV}}{n^2}.$$

parts.label: b.
parts.statement:
In a hypothetical modern day experiment, electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential $V$ into a cloud of cold atomic hydrogen (Figure 1-1).  A series of plates with aligned holes select a beam of scattered electrons moving perpendicular to the plates.  Immediately beyond the final plate, the electrons enter a uniform magnetic field $B$ perpendicular to the beam; they curve and strike a piece of film mounted on the final plate.

When the film is developed, a series of spots is observed (Figure 1-2).  The distances between the hole and the two most distant spots are measured.  You may assume that the film is large enough to have intercepted all of the electrons, i.e. that there are no spots farther from the hole than those shown.  The number of spots shown is not necessarily accurate.

Make the approximation that the mass of the hydrogen atom is much larger than the mass of the electron.  Assume that each electron scatters off only one atom, which is initially in the ground state (lowest energy state) and has negligible thermal velocity.

Determine:

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: The magnitude of the magnetic field $B$.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: The magnitude of the accelerating potential $V$.

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement: The total number of spots on the film.

solution.statement:
B1. a. The electrostatic force causes the centripetal acceleration that keeps the electron in its circular orbit around the proton. Since the proton is assumed to be very massive, reduced mass effects can be neglected.

$$m\frac{v^2}{r} = k\frac{e^2}{r^2}$$

where $m$ is the electron mass, $e$ is the electron charge, $v$ is its orbital velocity, $r$ is its orbital radius and $k$ is Coulomb’s constant. Multiplying by $r$ yields

$$mv^2 = k\frac{e^2}{r}$$

The angular momentum of an object moving in a circle is $L = mvr$.

Combining this with Bohr’s postulate $mvr = n\hbar$

Solving this for $mv^2$ $$mv^2 = \frac{1}{m}\left(\frac{n\hbar}{r}\right)^2.$$

$$\frac{1}{m}\left(\frac{n\hbar}{r}\right)^2 = k\frac{e^2}{r}$$

Solving this for $\dfrac{1}{r}$ $$\frac{1}{r} = \frac{mke^2}{(n\hbar)^2}.$$

The total energy $E$ is the sum of the electron’s kinetic and potential energy.

$$E_n = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - k\frac{e^2}{r} = -k\frac{e^2}{2r} = -\frac{m(ke^2)^2}{2(n\hbar)^2}.$$

Which is $$E_n = -\frac{(9.109 \times 10^{-31})\left[(8.99 \times 10^{9})(1.602 \times 10^{-19})^2\right]^2}{2n^2\left(6.63 \times 10^{-34}/(2\pi)\right)^2} = -\frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{n^2}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

b. i. As the electrons are accelerated through the potential difference $V$, they gained kinetic energy $eV$. The hydrogen is initially in its ground state $E_1$. After the collision the electron has kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv_n^2$ and the atom is in state $n$ with energy $E_n$. Applying energy conservation, we have

$$eV + E_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_n^2 + E_n. \qquad (\mathrm{B1\text{-}1})$$

The electron enters the magnetic field $B$ with velocity $v_n$ perpendicular to $\vec{B}$. The force on the electron causes it to move in a circular path with radius $r_n$.

$$ev_nB = m\frac{v_n^2}{r_n}.$$

Solving for $mv_n$ $$mv_n = eBr_n.$$

Combining with (B1-1), $$eV + E_1 = \frac{(eBr_n)^2}{2m} + E_n. \qquad (\mathrm{B1\text{-}2})$$

The two furthest out spots correspond to $n = 1$ and 2. The diameters of the paths are $2r_1 = 0.09491$ m and $2r_2 = 0.03980$ m. The radii are $r_1 = 0.04746$ m and $r_2 = 0.01990$ m

Writing (B1-2) for these two cases $$eV + E_1 = \frac{(eBr_1)^2}{2m} + E_1$$

or $$eV = \frac{(eBr_1)^2}{2m} \qquad (\mathrm{B1\text{-}3})$$

and $$eV + E_1 = \frac{(eBr_2)^2}{2m} + E_2 = \frac{(eBr_2)^2}{2m} + \frac{E_1}{2^2}$$

or $$\frac{(eBr_1)^2}{2m} - \frac{(eBr_2)^2}{2m} = -\frac{3E_1}{4}.$$

Solving for $B$

$$B = \sqrt{-\frac{3E_1m}{2e^2(r_1^2 - r_2^2)}} = \sqrt{-\frac{3(-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J})(9.109 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg})}{2(1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C})^2\left((0.04746\ \mathrm{m})^2 - (0.01990\ \mathrm{m})^2\right)}} = 2.50 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T}$$

ii. Substituting into (B1-3)

$$V = \frac{e(Br_1)^2}{2m} = \frac{(1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C})\left((2.50 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T})(0.09491\ \mathrm{m})/2\right)^2}{2(9.109 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg})} = 12.4\ \mathrm{V}$$

iii. The electron’s kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv_n^2$ after the collision has got to be greater than zero. Using $n$ to represent the maximum $n$ in (B1-1)

$$eV > E_n - E_1 = \frac{E_1}{n^2} - E_1 = -E_1\left(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\right).$$

Expressing the energies in electron volts, this is $12.4\ \mathrm{eV} > 13.6\ \mathrm{eV}\left(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\right)$

or $$\frac{13.6}{n^2} > 1.2$$

or $$13.6/1.2 = 11.3 > n^2.$$

The maximum number of spots is 3.

problems.title: B2
problems.statement: A very long solenoid has radius $b$, $n$ turns per unit length, and carries current $I$ as shown in the accompanying cross-sectional view.  The solenoid is firmly fixed in place and cannot rotate.

figures.caption: cross-sectional view
figures.alt: Cross-sectional view with x and y axes: three concentric circles; the inner one of radius a carries +Q, the middle one of radius b is the solenoid with a curved arrow showing counterclockwise current I, the outer one of radius c carries –Q.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ inside the solenoid, far from its ends?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the magnetic energy density $u_\mathrm{B}$ stored in the solenoid?
parts.statementAfter: There are two long cylindrical shells of length $h$ and mass $m$ coaxial to the solenoid – one, inside the solenoid at a radius $a$, carries a charge $+Q$, uniformly distributed over its surface;  the other, outside the solenoid at radius $c$, carries charge $–Q$.  $h \gg c$.  Use $r$ to represent the distance from the cylinders’ axis.  The cylinders are free to rotate about their axes.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: What is the electric field $\vec{E}$ between the cylindrical shells, far from their ends?

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: What is the electric energy density $u_\mathrm{E}$ stored between the shells?
parts.statementAfter: The current in the solenoid is gradually reduced from $I$ to zero at a constant rate, $\Delta I/\Delta t$.  The cylindrical shells begin to rotate.  Assume the magnetic field generated by the rotating cylindrical shells is negligible.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Calculate the gain in angular momentum of each cylinder about its axis when the current in the solenoid is reduced from $I$ to zero.

parts.label: f.
parts.statement:
In addition to storing energy, fields can also store linear momentum and angular momentum. The density of linear momentum stored in electromagnetic fields is

$$\varepsilon_0\vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$

Calculate the change in angular momentum of the electromagnetic fields about the cylinders’ axis as the current in the solenoid is reduced from $I$ to zero.

answer.note: The official solution prints the stored angular momentum −½Qμ₀nI(b² − a²)ẑ, which goes to zero; it labels this the change.

problems.statementAfterParts: *$\{$Suggested by a problem in Introduction to Electrodynamics, 3rd Ed., by David J. Griffiths (Prentice Hall, Upper Saddle River, New Jersey, 1999), page 359.$\}$*

solution.statement:
B2. a. Using $\hat{z}$ to represent a unit vector in the $z$-direction, $\vec{B} = \mu_0 nI\hat{z}$ for $r < b$. (It is not necessary to derive this result from Ampere’s Law.)

b. $$u_B = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2 = \frac{\mu_0 n^2 I^2}{2}.$$

It is also possible to derive this result from $U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$.

If edge effects are ignored $U = u_B hA$

where $h$ is the length and $A$ is the cross-sectional area of the solenoid. Combining this with $$LI = N\Phi = (nh)(BA)$$

yields $$u_B hA = \tfrac{1}{2}nhBAI,$$

or $$u_B = \tfrac{1}{2}nBI = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 n^2 I^2$$

c. The charge per unit length on the inner cylindrical shell is $\lambda = +Q/h$.

Letting $\hat{r}$ represent a unit vector in the $r$-direction, Gauss’s Law for cylindrical symmetry yields

$$\vec{E} = +\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 hr}\hat{r}.$$

d. $$u_E = \tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 = \frac{Q^2}{8\pi^2\varepsilon_0 h^2 r^2}.$$

e. Use Faradays Law to find the induced electric field at the location of each charged cylinder.

$$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.$$

$\vec{E}$ is constant around a circular path, the cross-section of the cylinder, $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = E2\pi r$.

The magnetic flux is $\Phi_B = BA$

where $A$ is the enclosed area that has a magnetic field. Thus

$$E2\pi r = -A\frac{dB}{dt} = -A\mu_0 n\frac{dI}{dt}.$$

Since $I$ is decreasing at a constant rate $$E2\pi r = -A\mu_0 n\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$$

For the inner cylinder, $r = a$ and $A = \pi a^2$, and $$E_a 2\pi a = -\pi a^2\mu_0 n\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}.$$

Therefore $$E_a = -\frac{\mu_0 na}{2}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}.$$

In order to oppose the decrease in $I$, $E$ is in the same direction as $I$

$$\vec{E}_a = -\frac{\mu_0 na}{2}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\hat{\phi}$$

For the outer cylinder, $r = c$ and $A = \pi b^2$, since the field $B = 0$ for $r > b$

and $$E_c 2\pi c = -\pi b^2\mu_0 n\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}.$$

Therefore $$E_c = -\frac{\mu_0 nb^2}{2c}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}.$$

with $$\vec{E}_c = -\frac{\mu_0 nb^2}{2c}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\hat{\phi}$$

Each cylinder experiences a torque caused by the electric force.

$$\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}_E.$$

For the inner cylinder $$\frac{d\vec{L}_a}{dt} = a\hat{r} \times Q\left(-\frac{\mu_0 na}{2}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\hat{\phi}\right) = -\frac{\mu_0 na^2Q}{2}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\hat{z}.$$

Since $I$ decreases at a constant rate, $L$ also changes at a constant rate.

$$\frac{\Delta\vec{L}_a}{\Delta t} = -\frac{\mu_0 na^2Q}{2}\frac{(0 - I)}{\Delta t}\hat{z}$$

$$\Delta\vec{L}_a = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 nIa^2Q\hat{z}.$$

For the outer cylinder $$\frac{d\vec{L}_c}{dt} = c\hat{r} \times (-Q)\left(-\frac{\mu_0 nb^2}{2c}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\hat{\phi}\right) = +\frac{\mu_0 nb^2Q}{2}\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\hat{z}.$$

and $$\frac{\Delta\vec{L}_c}{\Delta t} = +\frac{\mu_0 nb^2Q}{2}\frac{(0 - I)}{\Delta t}\hat{z}$$

$$\Delta\vec{L}_c = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_0 nIb^2Q\hat{z}.$$

f. $E = 0$ for $r < a$ and $B = 0$ for $r > b$. Using $\vec{\pi}_{EM}$ to represent the linear momentum density

$$\vec{\pi}_{EM} = \varepsilon_0\vec{E} \times \vec{B} = \varepsilon_0\left(\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 hr}\right)\hat{r} \times (\mu_0 nI)\hat{z} = -\frac{Q\mu_0 nI}{2\pi hr}\hat{\phi} \quad \text{for } a < r < b$$

and $$\vec{\pi}_{EM} = 0 \quad \text{for } r < a \text{ and } b < r$$

Using $\vec{\ell}_{EM}$ to represent the angular momentum density

$$\vec{\ell}_{EM} = \vec{r} \times \vec{\pi}_{EM}.$$

In the region $a < r < b$, $$\vec{\ell}_{EM} = \vec{r} \times \vec{\pi}_{EM} = (r\hat{r}) \times \left(-\frac{Q\mu_0 nI}{2\pi hr}\hat{\phi}\right) = -\frac{Q\mu_0 nI}{2\pi h}\hat{z}.$$

The angular momentum density is constant in the region $a < r < b$ and zero outside. Therefore the total angular momentum originally stored in the fields is

$$\vec{L}_{EM} = (\text{volume containing field})\,\vec{\ell}_{EM}$$

$$\vec{L}_{EM} = \left[h\pi(b^2 - a^2)\right]\left(-\frac{Q\mu_0 nI}{2\pi h}\hat{z}\right) = -\tfrac{1}{2}Q\mu_0 nI(b^2 - a^2)\hat{z}$$

When the current is reduced to zero, this angular momentum goes to zero. Therefore the change in angular momentum is

$$\vec{L}_{EM} = -\tfrac{1}{2}Q\mu_0 nI(b^2 - a^2)\hat{z}.$$
